rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act (criminal-record screening limits)
rules.requirement: A housing provider may not use an application that asks about criminal records, or ask orally or in writing, before making a conditional offer. Two exceptions apply: methamphetamine manufacture on federally assisted premises, and lifetime sex-offender registration. At no point may the provider evaluate any of these records: arrests or charges without conviction; expunged, pardoned, vacated or sealed records; or juvenile adjudications. After a conditional offer, the provider may consider only two kinds of record. The first is a conviction for murder, aggravated sexual assault, kidnapping, arson, human trafficking, the listed sexual offenses, or a crime requiring lifetime registration. The second is an indictable offense within a lookback period. A withdrawal of the offer requires a preponderance-of-evidence finding that it is necessary to fulfill a substantial, legitimate and nondiscriminatory interest. The provider must also make an individualized assessment against six listed factors. A withdrawal requires a written notice that states the specific reasons and offers a chance to appeal with evidence. The applicant may request, within 30 days, all information relied on. The provider must supply it free within 10 days. Before accepting any application fee, the provider must disclose in writing whether criminal history is reviewed, and that the applicant may submit evidence of inaccuracy or rehabilitation. Providers may not: publish advertisements that exclude people with records; require drug or alcohol tests; or seek consent to obtain drug-treatment records. Enforcement is by complaint to the Division on Civil Rights only, not in court. The Division first offers a 14-day mediation window. Penalties are tiered by prior violations. The director may also order return of the application fee and a payment of up to $1,000 to the applicant.
rules.key_value: Lookback after conditional offer: 6 years (1st degree), 4 years (2nd/3rd degree), 1 year (4th degree); no limit for listed serious crimes or lifetime registration. Penalties up to $1,000 / $5,000 / $10,000.

rules.title: Residential rental application fee cap ($50, CPI-adjusted)
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee above $50 to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes. Starting January 1 of the year after enactment (2027), the Director of Consumer Affairs adjusts the cap each year by the CPI-U for New York-Northern NJ-Long Island, All Items. The adjustment uses the 12 months ending October 31. The State Treasurer determines it by December 1, and it applies to fees charged from January 1 of the following year. It is made only if the CPI change is greater than zero. The Director publishes the current limit online. Penalties are up to $500 for a first offense, $750 for a second and $1,000 for each later offense. They are collected under the Penalty Enforcement Law in the Special Civil Part on complaint of the Director or the Attorney General. The amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant. The Director must adopt rules, including a mechanism for reporting violations.
rules.key_value: $50 maximum application fee (CPI adjustment begins January 1, 2027); penalties up to $500 / $750 / $1,000

rules.title: New Jersey Security Deposit Law
rules.requirement: A security deposit may not exceed 1.5 times one month's rent. Any pet deposit and any prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, count toward that cap. At lease start the landlord may collect at most 2.5 months in total: the deposit plus the first month's rent. Yearly increases in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. The deposit stays the tenant's property and must be held in trust, not commingled. Landlords holding deposits for fewer than 10 units must use an interest-bearing account at an insured NJ bank or savings and loan. Landlords with 10 or more units may instead use an insured NJ money-market fund. Interest belongs to the tenant and is paid annually in cash or as a rent credit. Within 30 days of receipt, and at each annual payment, the landlord must give written notice of the bank, the amount, the account type and the interest rate. If notice or interest is not provided, the tenant may apply the deposit plus 7% annual interest to rent. A 30-day cure period applies to missed annual notices. Within 30 days after the tenancy ends, the landlord must return the deposit plus interest, less itemized deductions. Deductions are limited to damage beyond normal wear and tear and other sums due under the lease. Return must be by personal delivery or registered or certified mail. Return is due within 5 business days if the tenant is displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation. It is due within 15 business days after a Safe Housing Act (domestic violence) termination. A tenant may sue for double the amount wrongfully withheld, plus costs and attorney's fees. A new owner is responsible for the deposit. Willful withholding from tenants on public assistance carries civil penalties of $500 to $2,000. Unlawful use of deposit money is a disorderly persons offense.

rules.title: New Jersey Anti-Eviction Act (good cause eviction)
rules.requirement:
A residential landlord may not evict a tenant, or fail to renew a written or oral lease, without good cause. The statutory causes (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(a)-(r)) are:
- nonpayment of rent
- disorderly conduct after a Notice to Cease
- willful or grossly negligent damage
- substantial breach of rules or lease covenants after a Notice to Cease
- failure to pay a rent increase that is not unconscionable and complies with municipal rent control
- health and safety violations, illegal occupancy or government redevelopment
- permanent retirement from residential use
- refusal of reasonable lease changes
- habitual late payment
- condominium, cooperative or fee-simple conversion
- owner or buyer occupancy after conversion, or in buildings of three or fewer units
- end of employment-based tenancy
- certain drug, assault, terroristic-threat, theft and human-trafficking offenses

A written Notice to Quit is required for every cause except nonpayment. The notice period runs from 3 days to 3 years depending on the cause. Only a court judgment and a warrant of removal executed by a court officer can remove a tenant; self-help eviction is illegal. Tenants evicted to correct an illegal occupancy are owed relocation assistance of six times monthly rent, with interest of 18% a year if unpaid where no municipal fund exists. A landlord who misuses a unit after an owner-occupancy eviction is liable for treble damages. A landlord who returns the property to residential use within 5 years of a retirement or demolition eviction faces treble damages and a civil penalty of up to $10,000. Rooming and boarding house owners must follow the same causes and notices and give the County Welfare Board 3 working days' notice. Unregistered landlords cannot obtain an eviction until they comply.
rules.key_value: Notice to Quit: 3 days (disorderly, damage, employment end, criminal causes); 1 month (rule or lease breach, rent increase, lease changes, habitual late payment); 2 months (post-conversion or small-building owner/buyer occupancy); 3 months (health and safety); 18 months (retirement from residential use); 3 years (conversion). Relocation 6x monthly rent for illegal occupancy; penalty up to $10,000.

coverage.owner_conditions: Owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings: eviction is allowed for holdover after lease expiry, nonpayment, disorderly conduct, willful damage, repeated rule violations, or lease violations where re-entry is reserved. Notice to quit is 3 months for at-will or year-to-year tenancies and 1 month for month-to-month tenancies. A 3-day notice applies for disorderly, destructive or rule-violation causes.
coverage.other_conditions: Hotel and motel guests with no alternate residence who live there continuously are covered. Landlords who are not properly registered cannot evict until they comply.

rules.exemptions: Transient or seasonal hotel, motel and guest-house guests; units held in trust for a developmentally disabled family member; owner-occupied two- and three-family dwellings are covered only by the narrower 2A:18-61.2(a) causes.

rules.title: Foreclosure tenant protections and notices (Foreclosure Fairness Act)
rules.requirement: Foreclosure alone is not grounds for eviction. A buyer of a foreclosed property who wants to occupy it as a primary residence must give a 90-day notice to quit. A tenant whose lease runs longer may not be evicted until the lease expires. Anyone acquiring a foreclosed property with residential rental units must notify tenants in English and Spanish within 10 business days of the sale. The notice must say that ownership has changed and that tenants need not move because of the foreclosure. It is delivered by door posting and by certified and regular mail. In buildings with more than 10 units it is posted in a prominent common location instead. Foreclosing creditors must give the court-rule notice of tenant rights. A monetary offer to induce a tenant to leave must be accompanied by the NOTICE TO TENANTS. The tenant's acceptance must be in writing and acknowledge a five-day review period. Pressure tactics are prohibited. These include misrepresenting rights, harassment, cutting utilities, failing to maintain the property, and unconscionable or rent-control-violating rent increases.

coverage.summary: Applies to residential rental units in foreclosed properties. Month-to-month tenants and owner-occupied two- and three-family units are not exempt from the 90-day notice. In buildings with more than 10 units, posting replaces individual notices.
coverage.other_conditions: Triggered only by foreclosure and transfer of title.

rules.effective_date_note: The guide states no effective date.

rules.review_note: The guide cites no statute for the 90-day notice to quit; it relies on Chase Manhattan Bank v. Josephson. The citations reflect the Foreclosure Fairness Act sections named for the notice duties and the bar on pressure tactics.

rules.title: Reprisal protections for tenants
rules.requirement:
A landlord may not retaliate against a tenant by eviction, by substantially altering the lease or its terms, or by refusing to renew. The protection covers a tenant who exercises any of these rights:
- enforcing rights under the lease or State or local law
- making a good-faith complaint to a government authority about a health or safety violation, after first notifying the landlord in writing and allowing reasonable time to correct it
- organizing or joining a lawful organization, including a tenant organization
- refusing lease changes made in retaliation for these acts

The tenant may sue for damages.

rules.title: Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act (conversion protections, including bar on conversion-cost rent increases)
rules.requirement: Some tenants in a building converted to condominium, cooperative or fee-simple ownership may obtain a protected tenancy that bars eviction for up to 40 years. Eligible tenants are those aged 62 or older before the recording date, those permanently disabled, and qualifying veterans with a service-connected disability of 60% or more. The tenant must have lived in the building at least one year before the conversion recording date. Family income must be no more than three times the county average per-person income or $50,000, whichever is greater. The landlord or converter must notify tenants of their right to apply. Applications are generally due within 60 days. For all tenants in a converting building, whether protected or not, rents may not be raised to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. Increases for new services or amenities remain allowed. In the protected-tenancy context, the landlord bears the burden of proving that lease changes are reasonable. The Tenant Protection Act of 1992 amendment (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.40 to -61.59) extends similar protected tenancy to qualified tenants in qualified counties who did not qualify as seniors or disabled persons. Hudson County is currently the only qualified county.

unverifiable_exemptions: Tenant eligibility: age 62+ before the recording date, permanent disability, or qualifying disabled veteran status

rules.title: Law Against Discrimination: source of lawful income and other protected characteristics in rental housing
rules.requirement: The Law Against Discrimination (LAD) bars discrimination in renting housing on these grounds: race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital, civil union or domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, mental or physical disability, nationality, and source of lawful income or of lawful rent or mortgage payment. For example, a landlord cannot deny a Section 8 voucher holder an apartment based solely on that source of income. Discriminatory advertising is barred. A landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income, poor credit history, an oversized family or a zoning-violating occupancy. A complaint may be filed with the Division on Civil Rights free within 180 days, or in Superior Court within two years. Penalties run up to $10,000 for a first offense.
rules.key_value: Complaint to DCR within 180 days (free) or Superior Court within 2 years; penalties up to $10,000 for a first offense

coverage.owner_conditions: Rental of a single apartment in a two-family dwelling whose other unit the owner occupies as a residence at the time of rental is exempt.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement:
The act makes the following unlawful, each as a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act:
- a rental property owner or its agent paying for, subscribing to or contracting for the services of a coordinator
- a coordinator facilitating a tacit or express agreement among rental property owners that restricts competition, including by performing a coordinating function
- two or more persons engaging in or facilitating parallel pricing coordination
- any person performing a coordinating function

A coordinating function is any one of the following:
- collecting nonpublic, competitively sensitive information from two or more owners for algorithmic processing used to set or recommend rents, lease terms or occupancy
- setting rents or terms with an algorithm that uses another owner's nonpublic data
- recommending rents to multiple owners through the same or a substantially similar algorithm

Antitrust Act remedies (N.J.S.A. 56:9-6 to 56:9-17) apply. The Attorney General must set up a complaint location and may adopt rules. Section 6(b) bars municipalities from enacting ordinances that conflict with the act.
rules.key_value: Effective July 1, 2027; violations are New Jersey Antitrust Act violations; conflicting municipal ordinances prohibited

coverage.landlord_size_condition: Applies to any rental property owner owning one or more rental residential dwelling units. Controlling-interest holders are treated as a single owner with the entity.
coverage.summary: Covers residential dwelling units (houses, apartments, accessory units and other primary residences) in New Jersey. Excludes inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care and detention or correctional facilities.
coverage.other_conditions: Not a coordinating function: research, statistics or testing not used to set terms; free public rent estimates; equal-terms brokerage listing databases that do not set or recommend rents; government affordability controls. Not an algorithmic device: spreadsheets operating without AI that require human analysis, and databases that only query unprocessed data.

rules.exemptions: Research, statistical or testing uses; free public rent estimates; equal-terms brokerage databases; government affordability controls (also excluded as coordinators); non-AI spreadsheets requiring human analysis; query-only databases.
